analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks from mega-investors who buy single-family homes and taxes their home sales at full value.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2026 with 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, the bill was referred to two House committees and has had no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets corporations and investment funds with more than $100 million in assets that buy up single-family homes to rent them out. It would take away the tax deductions — mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation — that make owning those homes profitable, and it would charge a tax equal to 100% of the sale price if one of these investors sells a home, effectively making it very expensive to buy and flip family homes. It also bars Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from backing mortgages for these large investors, cutting off cheap federal-backed financing for the practice. Money raised would go into a federal fund that builds affordable rental housing for very low-income families.
analysis.who_benefits: First-time homebuyers and ordinary renters who currently bid against deep-pocketed investors for single-family homes would face less competition and less upward pressure on prices and rents. Very low-income and homeless families would benefit if the bill's excise tax collections flow into the Housing Trust Fund to build affordable rentals.

how_it_helps.text: Large investors ($100M+ in assets, counting controlled affiliates) would lose the mortgage interest and insurance deductions and depreciation write-offs on single-family rental homes, raising their cost of holding family homes.
A new excise tax equal to 100% of the sale price would make it economically punishing for a large investor to buy and flip or hold single-family homes.

Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae would be barred from buying, lending on, or guaranteeing mortgages where the lender or owner is a large investor, cutting off the cheapest financing for the investor-landlord business model.
Money collected from the excise tax would go into the federal Housing Trust Fund to build and preserve rental housing for extremely low- and very low-income families, including homeless families.

analysis.who_pays: Investors with over $100 million in assets that own single-family rental homes bear the direct cost: lost deductions, a 100% tax on sales, and loss of Fannie/Freddie/Ginnie financing. Mortgage lenders and servicers that do business with these investors would lose that volume. Some tenants of large landlord operators could see higher rents or thinner maintenance if operators absorb the higher costs.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax equals 100% of the sale price, so a large investor would have to pay the government the entire proceeds to sell a home. That could trap big landlords in their existing holdings rather than push them to sell to families, freezing the status quo instead of unwinding it.

Stripping mortgage interest and depreciation deductions raises the cost of holding rental homes, and some of that cost could be passed on to tenants through higher rents or reduced maintenance before the tax provisions take effect.

The bill targets ownership, not construction of new homes. It exempts newly built or substantially rehabilitated properties, but critics could argue it does little on its own to increase the overall supply of housing, which many economists see as the root of the affordability problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — making it unprofitable for $100M+ investors to own entry-level homes — is real and would matter to buyers and renters priced out by investor competition. But the design is blunt: a 100% excise tax on the sale price makes it prohibitively expensive for a large investor to sell, which could freeze their existing homes in place rather than move them to families, and stripping depreciation and interest deductions could squeeze renters if operators cut maintenance or raise rents to compensate. The bill is more likely to deter new investor purchases than to unwind existing portfolios, and it does little to directly build homes except through the trust fund and the construction exception. Honest supporters would acknowledge the bill is a signal as much as a working market intervention, and that it would need committee refinement to avoid entrenching the very landlords it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees when introduced and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no vote, no movement.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 16, 2026, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee, which share jurisdiction over its tax and housing-finance provisions.
The only recorded actions since introduction are the referral itself; no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.
All 18 original supporters (the sponsor and 17 cosponsors) are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and House rules give the majority control over whether any bill reaches the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutional landlords and corporate home-buying investors are better off so far, because the bill sits untouched in committee and their tax deductions and financing access remain intact. Renters and first-time buyers gain nothing yet.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in January 2026 and assembled 17 Democratic cosponsors; the bill was sent to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees.

for.name: 17 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors including Watson Coleman, Deluzio, Garcia, Tlaib, Frost, and Takano
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; no Republican cosponsor joined.

against.name: Institutional single-family rental industry
against.role: Corporate landlords and home-buying investment firms
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have publicly opposed earlier versions of this same proposal, arguing it would disrupt housing markets, and no member of Congress from either party has moved the bill toward a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 supporters at introduction are Democrats; no Republican cosponsor has joined, and with the House majority controlling committee agendas, the bill has seen no action beyond referral.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental landlords and corporate home investors
industries.note: These investors would lose the interest, insurance, and depreciation deductions that make owning family homes profitable, face a 100%-of-price tax on any sale, and lose access to Fannie, Freddie, and Ginnie financing. The bill is written specifically to make their business model unworkable, which would lower the investor bid on entry-level homes.

industries.industry: Mortgage finance (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae guarantee businesses)
industries.note: The bill bars the mortgage giants from buying, guaranteeing, or securitizing loans tied to large-investor landlords, removing a slice of their volume. Their continued access to that business runs against homebuyers, since it is government-backed financing that subsidizes investor competition for family homes.

industries.industry: Low-income renters and the affordable housing sector (Housing Trust Fund)
industries.note: Excise tax collections would flow to the Housing Trust Fund to build and preserve rentals for extremely low-income and homeless families, a direct benefit to the people least able to compete in tight housing markets.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support and no committee action beyond referral to two committees, the bill is following the usual path for housing-investor proposals: it is likely to sit in committee without a hearing or vote for the rest of this Congress. Its realistic chance of advancing would require either a Democratic House majority or attachment to a larger tax or housing package, neither of which appears on the horizon.
